data.title: Carved Najdi Doors Reflect Local Architectural Heritage and Craftsmanship
data.content:
Buraidah, November 20, 2026, SPA -- The woodwork of Najdi doors, with its geometric patterns and plant motifs, tells part of the story of traditional architecture in Najd. Artisans passed the craft from one generation to the next, drawing on the beauty of their surroundings. In their hands, doors built to protect homes became works of art that express Najdi cultural identity and reflect how people lived and what they valued.
    Artisans traditionally worked with local materials, chiefly tamarisk wood and palm trunks, using the qualities of each to make doors that were both durable and beautiful. As social and economic conditions changed, so did the way artisans built and decorated the doors. New materials and techniques brought greater variety to their designs.
    The doors owe much of their beauty to patterns that artisans drew from nature and from symbols handed down through generations. Among the best known is the sunflower, a circular motif at the center of some doors. Grape clusters evoke hospitality and generosity, while palm fronds echo the trees of the local landscape. Raindrops, "Baythana" (cardamom pod), "Qeetan" (a braided band), and crowns give the designs variety and balance.
    Artisan Ahmed Al-Fawzan, who trains apprentices to make Najdi doors at the Royal Institute of Traditional Arts (Wrth), explained that the door carvings of Hail, Qassim, and Riyadh reflect each region’s distinctive style. In the past, he noted, such patterns adorned both doors and plasterwork, particularly in men’s reception rooms known as "Al Qahwa."
    Al-Fawzan described working with Wrth on its Apprenticeship in Najdi Door Construction, which admits a new group of students about every 18 months. By teaching students to make the doors, the program aims to preserve the carved designs and their original names and pass the skills of the craft on to future generations.
    -- SPA
